stories.title: Pinnacle Group Sells Rights to Upper West Side Apartment Tower for $88M
stories.excerpt: Pinnacle Group has offloaded another asset, this time on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. The prominent New York City landlord, which put a massive rent-stabilized portfolio into bankruptcy last year, sold its rights to an apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to private real estate company Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The Real Deal first reported the sale, citing filings by Pinnacle’s parent company, Zarasai Group, with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The filings, dated Aug. 13, announced the successfully completed sale of Pinnacle’s 100 percent interest in the 15-story building’s lease rights and a 50 percent hold on the land rights. Daniel Parker, Gary Phillips and Will Silverman at Eastdil Secured Savills advised on the deal. An $11 million surplus from the sale is slated to be deposited into the account of Series C bondholders. A spokesperson for Pinnacle Group could not be reached for comment on the most recent sale. The property carried an existing loan balance of about $65 million as of late March, last transferred from Starwood Mortgage Capital to a Barclays-sponsored commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) trust in 2023. Pinnacle secured the leasehold to 323 West 96th Street in 2007, according to city records, and paid another $27 million for its land rights stake in 2016. The 173-unit apartment building, built in 2001, sits at the corner of East 96th Street and First Avenue. The sale comes days after news that Pinnacle offloaded a $128 million condominium and commercial portfolio spanning 39 transactions across Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. The buyer was Friar Park JW, an entity with links to Tremada Holdings, an affiliate of London-based property company William Pears Group. Pinnacle, led by Joel Wiener, placed a portfolio of roughly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments across New York City into bankruptcy in May 2025 after facing approximately $574.4 million in debt. stories.summary: Pinnacle Group, the rent-stabilized landlord in bankruptcy reorganization, sold its leasehold and 50% land rights to the 15-story Upper West Side apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million. The sale generated an $11 million surplus after satisfying the existing $65 million loan balance, with proceeds directed to Series C bondholders. This represents Pinnacle's continued liquidation of distressed assets.
stories.impact: Distressed multifamily asset sales in Manhattan signal portfolio stress among stabilized-housing operators but create acquisition opportunities for well-capitalized buyers like Lightstone. The $88M valuation on a 15-story rent-stabilized asset reflects compressed returns typical of NYC's regulatory environment; developers should monitor similar forced sales on the Upper West Side and across Manhattan as a potential source of off-market acquisition opportunities or land parcels.

stories.title: At New York City Council Hearing on Pied-à-Terre Tax, Complaints of a Sloppy Rollout

Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer led the inquiry against what she saw as a dysfunctional rollout of the tax that included publishing up to 900,000 names and addresses of possible second homes in the five boroughs. The Mamdani administration did not send any representatives to the hearing at City Hall, including from the Department of Finance tasked with collecting the tax. The hearing was held by the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. “No estimate of the number of pied-à-terres in the city comes even close to 900,000,” Brewer said. “Yet, the city still published the list with the small caveat that the properties on the list may be subject to the charge. The list published by the Department of Finance was so overbroad that it even included my name, and I don’t mind my name and my home address [being included], but I’ve been in that home 365 days a year since 1994. I don’t leave the city, and I don’t have a second home.” The committee hoped to get answers from the Mamdani administration on why — when it had credible information from the New York City Comptroller‘s office about how many second homes there are — it still attempted to force thousands of property owners in the city to prove that the addresses are primary residences. stories.summary: New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday examining the rollout of the city's pied-à-terre tax, with Councilmember Gale Brewer leading criticism of the Department of Finance's overbroad publication of approximately 900,000 property addresses and names as potential second homes. The administration sent no representatives to defend the implementation, and the council raised concerns that the published list vastly overstated actual second-home inventory. Legal battles over the tax's constitutionality remain ongoing.
stories.impact: The pied-à-terre tax's bungled rollout and ongoing legal challenges create pricing uncertainty in Manhattan's high-end residential market, potentially depressing investment demand and delaying capital deployment into luxury multifamily development. Developers should track tax litigation outcomes closely, as adverse rulings could shift investor appetite back toward Manhattan rental development, while sustained implementation could reduce investor competition for trophy assets and create valuation discounts.

stories.title: Vivmark Residential Launches with $70B Enterprise Value
stories.excerpt: Shares of Vivmark Residential were up Tuesday afternoon following the launch of trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the VMRK ticker. The merger of equals between Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities, creating an apartment REIT with a market capitalization of $51 billion and an enterprise value of $70 billion, was finalized Monday. “Our vision is to be the most trusted and best-performing rental housing company in America and one that gets better as it grows,” said Benjamin Schall, CEO of Vivmark. “Our wider management team of Vivmark officers is now fully in place, and we are ready to deliver a seamless Day 1 experience for our residents.” In addition to Schall, the Vivmark executive team includes Michael Manelis as COO and Kevin O’Shea as CFO. The board includes seven trustees from each company and is led by chairman Stephen Sterrett. Vivmark is dual headquartered in Arlington, VA and Chicago. The post Vivmark Residential Launches with $70B Enterprise Value appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Equity Residential + AvalonBay merger closes; creates Vivmark with $70B enterprise value

stories.summary: Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities completed their merger of equals on Monday, creating Vivmark Residential, a new apartment REIT with a $51 billion market capitalization and $70 billion enterprise value. Trading began Tuesday on the NYSE under ticker VMRK. The combined company is led by CEO Benjamin Schall and COO Michael Manelis, with headquarters in Arlington, Virginia and Chicago.
stories.impact: The creation of a $70B-EV megaREIT consolidates significant multifamily development and management capacity, potentially accelerating land acquisition and capital deployment in key markets where both predecessors operated (especially Sunbelt, Midwest, and coastal metros). Watch for Vivmark's 2025 guidance on development starts, cap rates, and same-store NOI growth—signals that will shape debt availability, construction costs, and yield requirements across the multifamily sector.

stories.title: Irvine Company’s Chicago Office Portfolio 87% Leased Amid Market Momentum
stories.excerpt: Irvine Company announced an increase in leasing activity, bringing its national office portfolio to 91% leased. Irvine Company closed its fiscal year with 11 million square feet of leasing activity, including 4.4 million square feet of new leasing and 6.7 million square feet of renewals. In its Chicago office portfolio, Irvine Company is 87% leased, including activity from financial services and legal services companies. “Our strong leasing activity reflects a clear market trend: companies are actively seeking high-quality environments that bring teams together,” said Roger DeWames, President of Irvine Company Office Properties. “We see continued strong demand for the value and scale we offer, driven by our commitment to continually investing in our premium workplaces and adapting alongside our customers as their business needs change.” Irvine Company completed a new full floor of flex suites at 300 North LaSalle this summer. The move-in-ready workspaces range from 4,500 to 10,000 square feet and offer access to the building’s enterprise amenities. bullets: Irvine Company's Chicago office portfolio 87% leased; national office 91% leased
11M SF leasing activity in fiscal year; 4.4M SF new, 6.7M SF renewals
Financial and legal services driving Chicago leasing; flex workspace demand strong
stories.summary: Irvine Company reported strong office leasing momentum, bringing its national portfolio to 91% occupancy and its Chicago office portfolio to 87% leased, driven primarily by financial services and legal services firms. The company closed its fiscal year with 11 million square feet of leasing activity (4.4M new, 6.7M renewal) and recently completed a new flex-suite offering at 300 North LaSalle ranging from 4,500 to 10,000 SF.
stories.impact: Office market stabilization in Chicago does NOT directly benefit multifamily developers but signals selective corporate hiring and workplace consolidation among white-collar employers—a precursor to residential demand growth if legal and finance hiring continues. Monitor Chicago's downtown office recovery closely; sustained occupancy gains and flex-space growth could drive young professional in-migration and strengthen demand for Class A rental apartments in River North, West Loop, and South Loop submarkets.

stories.title: Albany Road Snags Loan for Scottsdale MOB Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield has arranged $19.9 million in acquisition financing for Edwards Professional Park I & II in Scottsdale. Tyler Morss of Cushman & Wakefield’s Healthcare Capital Markets team arranged the debt through an undisclosed regional bank on behalf of the borrower, Albany Road. Located at 10752 N. 89th Place and 8952 E. Desert Cove Ave., Edwards Professional Park I & II features 91,469 square feet spread across two buildings. At the time of the loan closing, the buildings were currently 91% leased to 47 medical and healthcare-related tenants. Approximately 98.7% of the occupied space is dedicated to healthcare uses, including dentistry, orthopedics, gastroenterology, dermatology, behavioral health, physical medicine, infusion therapy and aesthetic medicine practices. Albany Road has made 110 investments since its inception in 2012 across a wide range of product types, geographies, and tenant profiles. The post Albany Road Snags Loan for Scottsdale MOB Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Albany Road arranges $19.9M acquisition loan for Scottsdale medical office buildings

stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield arranged $19.9 million in acquisition financing through an undisclosed regional bank for Albany Road's purchase of Edwards Professional Park I & II in Scottsdale. The two-building medical office portfolio totals 91,469 square feet and is 91% leased to 47 healthcare-related tenants, with 98.7% of occupied space dedicated to healthcare services across diverse specialties.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. However, strong healthcare real estate fundamentals and regional bank lending appetite in Phoenix signal investor confidence in Scottsdale submarkets; this confidence may extend to mixed-use or transit-adjacent multifamily projects that capture healthcare-worker demand and downtown office clusters.

stories.title: Betting on South Beach Luxury Shopping, Vivienne Westwood Plans to Open Store
stories.excerpt: Vivienne Westwood is finally getting serious about opening a boutique in Miami’s South Beach. Almost two years after buying the three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue and letting it sit vacant, the luxury fashion brand has submitted an application to build out the property, which dates back to 1921. The 4,356-square-foot ground-floor space would feature a store with three fittings rooms and two storage rooms. The second floor would house executive offices and meeting rooms, while the top floor would include a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. A neon sign would be mounted onto the entrance wall. The project “honors the building’s 1921 Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival heritage while introducing contemporary elements,” wrote Daniel Gabay, who runs National Permit Group and filed the proposal. The modern elements include “Florida limestone cladding, polished brass storefront and motifs, a rigid canopy reinterpreting the documented historic faux eave, a landmark pink neon signature, and the iconic Orb statue in the forecourt,” per the application, which Miami Beach Historic Preservation Board will consider next month. In 2024, the British brand paid $6 million for the 14,692-square-foot building located just a few blocks west of Ocean Drive, sandwiched between Seventh and Eighth Streets. Unlike most luxury labels of its size, it remains independent under the ownership of Vivienne Westwood’s family. The namesake designer passed away in 2022. Vivienne Westwood, the brand, is betting that high-end retail will return to the heart of South Beach. In the 1990s and 2000s, the area housed boutiques from the likes of Versace, Hugo Boss and Barney’s. But almost all shuttered, opting instead to open outposts at the Bal Harbour Shops up north and the Design District out west, which have become some of the highest-grossing upscale malls in the country. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Vivienne Westwood submits buildout plan for 4,356 SF flagship at 736 Collins Ave, South Beach

stories.summary: Vivienne Westwood has submitted a buildout application for its three-story boutique flagship at 736 Collins Avenue in Miami's South Beach, nearly two years after acquiring the vacant 1921 Art Deco property. The 4,356-square-foot ground floor will house a retail store with fittings and storage; upper floors will include executive offices and a bridal showroom with rooftop deck. The design blends historic preservation with contemporary elements including Florida limestone cladding and a signature pink neon sign.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. However, Vivienne Westwood's long-delayed South Beach retail activation signals tentative retailer confidence in Collins Avenue's recovery post-pandemic; watch for similar luxury brand commitments as leading indicators of tourist and foot-traffic recovery, which can support ground-floor retail economics in mixed-use residential developments along South Beach corridors.

stories.title: Northmarq Secures $51M Refinancing for Potomac Grocery-Anchored Property
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Washington, DC Debt + Equity team, led by Jason Smith and Kenneth Gentzel, arranged $50.75 million in permanent fixed-rate financing for Potomac Place Shopping Center. Potomac Place Shopping Center is an 80,040-square-foot grocery-anchored retail property located at 10100 River Road in Potomac, Maryland. Northmarq arranged financing on behalf of the borrower, Zuckerman Gravely, through its relationship with Nationwide Life Insurance Company. The permanent fixed-rate financing is structured on a seven-year term and will refinance existing debt on the property. Originally constructed in 1967, Potomac Place Shopping Center has served as an established neighborhood retail destination within the North Bethesda/Potomac submarket. The retail property is anchored by Safeway and features a mix of national and local tenants that provide a variety of shopping, dining and service offerings. Tenants include Safeway, Walgreens, Starbucks, Chipotle, Vie de France Bakery & Café, Strosnider’s Hardware, M&T Bank, PNC Bank, Maurizio’s, Duke’s Grocery, and The Market at River Falls. The post Northmarq Secures $51M Refinancing for Potomac Grocery-Anchored Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq arranges $50.75M permanent fixed-rate financing for Potomac Place Shopping Center

stories.summary: Northmarq secured $50.75 million in permanent fixed-rate financing through Nationwide Life Insurance for Potomac Place Shopping Center, an 80,040-square-foot grocery-anchored retail property in Potomac, Maryland, on behalf of borrower Zuckerman Gravely. The seven-year fixed-rate term refinances existing debt on the 1967-built property, which is anchored by Safeway and serves the North Bethesda/Potomac submarket.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily relevance. However, the willingness of institutional lenders (Nationwide Life) to refinance legacy suburban grocery-anchored centers at fixed rates suggests stable cap rates and property-level cash flow support in Washington DC suburbs; this lending appetite may extend to multifamily developments anchoring similar suburban mixed-use centers in the North Bethesda/Potomac corridor.

stories.title: Lathrop GPM LLP Completes Move to New DC Office
stories.excerpt: Lathrop GPM LLP’s Washington, D.C. team has relocated to a new 7,000-square-foot office on the 10th floor of 1015 15th Street NW. “We’re excited to move into a new office space that provides our team members and clients with a modern, flexible environment in the heart of Washington, D.C.” said Frank Sciremammano, partner in charge of the firm’s D.C. office. The law firm, which is based in Kansas City, downsized as part of the move from nearly 16,000 square feet at the Watergate. Located in the heart of Washington, D.C.’s central business district, the firm’s new office offera convenient access to major transit hubs, government institutions and business corridors, as well as cultural and dining destinations. Newmark represented Lathrop in the new office space deal. Over the last several years, Lathrop has relocated 10 regional offices to reduce overall costs. “Our real estate strategy is focused on providing environments that enable our professionals to do their best work and deliver exceptional value to clients,” said Chief Operating Officer Courtney Landon. The post Lathrop GPM LLP Completes Move to New DC Office appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lathrop GPM LLP downsizes DC office from 16K SF to 7K SF at 1015 15th St NW

stories.summary: Law firm Lathrop GPM LLP relocated its Washington, D.C. office to a new 7,000-square-foot space on the 10th floor of 1015 15th Street NW, downsizing from approximately 16,000 square feet at the Watergate. The move is part of a firm-wide cost-reduction strategy that has included relocation of 10 regional offices. The new space emphasizes modern, flexible work environments with proximity to transit, government institutions, and business corridors.
stories.impact: Office downsizing and flex-workspace adoption by major law firms signals post-pandemic occupancy normalization in DC's CBD and reduced large-floor-plate demand. This trend may free up Class A office space for adaptive conversion to residential or mixed-use; monitor DC's office pipeline for conversion candidates that could supply higher-density, transit-rich multifamily apartments in the central business district.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Vickey Barron of Compass
stories.excerpt: Vickey Barron, an associate broker at Compass, knows how to get deals done — and all with the perfect mix of intelligence, charm, charisma and a take-no-nonsense attitude. It’s what makes her one of the best real estate brokers in the business. Barron, 69, has worked on more than 600 sales during her career and earned a slew of awards, including the Real Estate Board of New York’s Rookie of the Year award in 2001 and the board’s Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award in 2015. Barron has done an endless amount of million-dollar deals, but for her, the value of her job isn’t money — it’s the difference she can make in someone’s life. “People always want me to talk about commissions and big sales, and I just am a strong believer that our purpose in this role of real estate is not money and commission and who has the biggest numbers,” Barron said. “It’s really about serving people.” Commercial Observer caught up with Barron in August for a new series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What was the biggest deal of your career? Vickey Barron: Ironically, this is not the one with the highest sale price or largest commission. In our business, there tends to be an emphasis on the commissions and money earned, but, going back to basics, we are in the business of helping people find homes and find solace. My biggest and most important deal was helping a 93-year-old woman negotiate a life estate so she could remain in her West Village townhouse after the sale took place. Sometimes we get caught up and forget that we’re all human and we age. Life has chapters, and our contributions matter. This deal had the biggest and most positive impact in my career. She emphasizes serving clients' life needs over maximizing transaction volume and commissions.

stories.title: Green Street Expands Student Housing Data Platform
stories.excerpt: Investors eyeing student housing assets have a newly expanded study tool. College House, a destination for specialized data and analytics on the U.S. student housing sector, is officially offering investors and operators direct access to analytics firm Green Street’s investment analytics. The platform expansion launched on Tuesday, a little more than a year after Green Street acquired College House in 2025. The news comes amid a complicated cooling period for the U.S. student housing market, according to Green Street’s own 2026 student housing report. Asset values have declined recently due to rising cap rates, while revenue growth is expected to average just 2 percent over the next two years, slightly trailing apartments. Capital is returning to student housing, according to commercial real estate finance firm Walker & Dunlop’s annual outlook, but is similarly selective, and activity remains below 2022 peaks. Construction starts are slowing and deliveries are highly concentrated, with the market splitting along enrollment trends. College House users can now tap Green Street estimates tailored to the student housing market within its platform, including key metrics like cap rates, risk-adjusted return estimates, occupancy and supply. The announcement also introduced a proprietary scoring framework, dubbed University Grades, that identifies long-term rent growth potential for nearly 180 U.S. schools. “This is exactly the integration we envisioned when we acquired College House,” Andrew McCulloch, chief analytics officer of Green Street, said in a statement. “Combining Green Street’s independent research and proprietary valuation framework with College House’s best-in-class data assets, will provide student housing investors a complete toolkit to allocate capital more effectively.” Time for investors to hit the books. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Green Street expands College House platform with proprietary investment analytics
College House acquired by Green Street in 2025; platform launched Tuesday
Student housing market cooling: cap rates rising, 2-year revenue growth ~2% expected
stories.summary: College House, a specialized student housing data and analytics platform acquired by Green Street in 2025, officially launched expanded analytics tools on Tuesday offering direct access to Green Street's investment analytics. According to Green Street's 2026 student housing report, the U.S. student housing sector is experiencing a cooling period marked by rising cap rates and declining asset values, with revenue growth expected to average just 2 percent over the next two years—slightly below multifamily apartment trends.
stories.impact: Student housing investment cooling signals capital selectivity and rising development hurdle rates in campus-adjacent markets. Developers should monitor student housing cap rate divergence from core multifamily; if the spread widens beyond 100 bps, purpose-built student housing becomes a marginal product, potentially freeing land parcels for traditional multifamily development or pushing sponsors toward mixed-demographic hybrid products in college towns.
